#1498. Glasner made to wait for first win as Trafford thwarts Forest

James Trafford became the record signing for a British goalkeeper this summer and he is already proving invaluable for Leeds United.

Signed from Manchester City for an initial £40m in August, Trafford has made an outstanding start and frustrated Nottingham Forest twice in four days.

The England international secured his second successive clean sheet in this City Ground sequel to underline why Leeds moved to eclipse the previous record for Jordan Pickford.

“England’s No 1” was a frequent chant from the travelling Leeds fans and although it may take some time for him to dislodge Pickford as the country’s first-choice, he is loving life at his new club.

Trafford produced a number of fine saves and goals from Daniel James and James Justin secured a comfortable Carabao Cup second-round victory for Leeds, who also won here in the league on Saturday.

Dan James has put Leeds ahead against Nottingham Forest 💥 pic.twitter.com/BdiYMXFJ5h

Leeds manager Daniel Farke said: “He has the potential to be one of the best goalkeepers in the Premier League and that is why Thomas Tuchel has picked him for England.

“I like his natural confidence and aura, he knows that he’s good and he will be outstanding one day.

“He has major chances to be under the spotlight and we are very pleased with him so far.”

Forest manager Oliver Glasner will be pleased to see the back of Leeds. He was appointed by Forest for the primary reason of winning trophies after successful tenures with Crystal Palace and Eintracht Frankfurt, but this particular avenue is now closed for this season.

Four-time League Cup winners, Forest endured a difficult evening following the pre-match news that they have agreed a £45m deal with Chelsea for striker Liam Delap.

Forest have established a reputation for noisy transfer windows but are determined to focus on quality over quantity this year. With Delap to undergo a medical on Wednesday, Forest will then focus on signing a new right wing-back before the deadline.

Newcastle’s Jacob Murphy has been discussed, though a move is now regarded as unlikely. There are understood to be other targets under consideration.

Glasner has insisted he does not want Forest to panic, and it remains to be seen whether they do spring into life on the final day. He said: “I am not a magician or the messiah and we cannot ignore the reality that Leeds are ahead of us at the moment.

“For nine months last season we were fighting relegation, so the players know it is going to take a lot of work. I know exactly what we have to change and that is what we will do.

“We are responsible and made so many mistakes. Maybe we needed this result. At the moment we are far away from what we want but we will get there.”

This was a more open game than the attritional encounter from last weekend, as Trafford was forced into a fine early save to prevent Ola Aina’s cross from arcing into the top corner.

Yet both teams were frequently making mistakes and providing masterclasses in how to misplace passes, frustrating their respective managers in the technical area.

The most impressive moment of the first-half came from Leeds centre-back Joe Rodon, racing back into position to deny Chris Wood from close range. Rodon celebrated the tackle as if it were a 30-yard screamer.

It was always likely to be a mistake which proved the pivotal moment, and Arnaud Kalimuendo’s poor header cost the home team in the 50th minute.

Kalimuendo’s error presented Sean Longstaff with space to run into and his pass found James, who beat Matz Sels with a clinical finish.

“Can we play you every week?” was the inevitable chant from the travelling Leeds supporters.

Forest’s fans were becoming twitchy and Trafford produced another save to frustrate Wood from eight yards after a break down the right from Kalimuendo.

Glasner responded by making a quadruple substitution on the hour, yet Leeds remained dangerous and added a second goal 15 minutes from time when Justin bundled home after a goalmouth scramble.

Ethan Ampadu's long throw causes CHAOS in the Forest box as Leeds go 2-0 up! pic.twitter.com/CtGDDIaRNp

You can catch the draw for the next stage of the League Cup on Sky Sports Main Event tomorrow night after the conclusion of Preston North End vs Everton.

Nottingham Forest have agreed a club-record deal worth £45m for Chelsea forward Liam Delap.

Delap has been deemed surplus to requirements at Stamford Bridge, and while the clubs were in talks over an initial loan deal, they have now struck a permanent agreement for the striker.

The 23-year-old​ only signed for Chelsea in a £30m deal from Ipswich Town 12 months ago​ ​and is scheduled for a medical on Wednesday​. He will become Forest’s most expensive signing with the deal eclipsing the £37.5m they paid for Omari Hutchinson last summer.

Oliver Glasner has prioritised the addition of a new forward and Delap was a long-term target for the Austrian since his time as Crystal Palace head coach.

Delap held talks with Forest last year over a potential move, and was also understood to have spoken with Glasner while he was at Palace.

Speaking to ITV after the win, Rodon said: “I thought we were a bit sharper going forward, maybe a bit naive in the first half. I thought we had a lot of good chances maybe could have scored a couple of goals but we know it’s a difficult place to come and overall very happy to keep a clean sheet and win the game.”

Of his last-ditch tackle in the first half, he added: “We love it, as defenders it’s as good as a goal. I’m delighted, [keeping] clean sheets is my job and overall I got it right in the end.”

"There's a healthy arrogance about Leeds""Farke has gone from strength to strength"Izzy Christiansen and Jobi McAnuff praise the impact of Daniel Farke at Leeds 📈 pic.twitter.com/fgzLWRk3U2

"It's a bit soon to say Wembley!" 😅James Justin and Dan James react to Leeds progressing into round three of the Carabao Cup 🎙️ pic.twitter.com/m81C6eJT7C

And that is it. Two home defeats by Leeds in less than 80 hours for Forest. Glasner will have much to ponder with a daunting trip to Anfield coming up on Saturday. All smiles for Farke’s side.

A look at a third for Leeds. Aaronson drives forward before setting Wilson who in turn lays on a first-time pass to Calvert-Lewin. The forward attempts to take his shot first time but can’t get the requisite power on the ball to beat Sels.

A pitch invader makes a brief appearance on the turf but is swiftly ushered away.

There is a late chance for Forest. Hutchinson’s cross is helped on by Dominguez but that touch inadvertently takes the ball away from Ndoye at the back post.

Forest fans are filing out of the exits and who can blame them?

That just about sums up Forest’s night. Dominguez stands over a free-kick from a dangerous area and, with the box loaded with their most imposing aerial threats, the midfielder sends the ball well over their heads and out for a goal-kick. So poor.

Calvert-Lewin is now on for Nmecha. Not really the striker Forest defenders would want to see at this stage of the game.

Another set-piece, this time a Stach corner, is barely dealt with by Forest.

There’s a shout for a handball at the other end as Ndoye spears a cross into the body of Elvedi, but the referee rightly waves the appeals away.

The “oles” ring out from the away end as Leeds string a series of passes together in the corner right in front of it. Forest are looking rather helpless here.

Nottingham Forest 0 Leeds United 2 (Justin) Ampadu launches a throw-in from the right but has to reload as the referee notices some pushing in the box. His next attempt is far too loopy but causes Forest all sorts of trouble, bouncing and bobbling, and coming all the way through a thicket of limbs to Nmecha at the far post. Williams attempts to keep the ball out from a prone position on the goalline under pressure from Justin, who gets the final touch as the ball is bundled over the line.

It's messy but Leeds won't care! 😁Forest fail to deal with the throw-in and Nmecha is there to bundle it in...#EFL | #CarabaoCup pic.twitter.com/oV46fs5RmP

Jair goes into the book after catching Ampadu in full flight. He never had a prayer of reaching that ball.

The resulting free-kick lands to Amapadu himself in the box, but his effort is deflected behind for a corner which is not up to much.

Goalscorer James is taken off for Bogle, who will offer more mettle down Leeds’ right side as Forest search for an equaliser in the closing stages.

Stach has only been on the field for a matter of seconds but comes within a few inches of scoring. Wilson does well on the edge of the box before laying the ball to Stach whose curled effort grazes the outside of the side-netting.

Longstaff’s final contribution to this game is a foul and yellow card as he spreads his legs wide to stop Ndoye breaking away through the middle.

He is replaced by Wilson, as Tanaka and Okafaor also make way, for Stach and Aaronson.

There’s plenty more endeavour down Forest’s new-look left side. Hudson Odoi scampers down that flank before cutting inside, and while he’s unable to fashion a chance the intent is correct.

The substitutions appear to have breathed life into this Forest side. Murillo picks out Dominguez charging forward and Trafford does well to tip the midfielder’s effort behind. The resulting corner comes to nothing.

Glasner resolves he has seen enough and rings the changes. Diomande, Aina, Jesus and Kalimuendo are replaced by Murillo, Netz, Ndoye and Hudson Odoi.

Okafor shows off his dancing feet in the Forest box, pulling off a few stepovers before the ball comes to Ampadu on the edge of the area but his strike is dragged wide.

Chances at both ends! Kalimuendo plays a wonderful ball into the box for Wood to sweep home but Trafford springs into action and makes a stunning save.

Leeds go up the other end, Okafor profiting from a diversionary run from centre-back Elvedi but cannot find the target and double Forest’s lead.

End-to-end football! ⚡️First Wood, then Okafor - just 19 seconds between the two chances 😮#EFL | #CarabaoCup pic.twitter.com/TGQmtwLNwE

Leeds are ahead and the inevitable chant from the away supporters is “can we play you every week?”

This is of course their second meeting in four days and Leeds are on course to record the double.

Forest’s fans are starting to get a little twitchy.

Dan James puts Leeds United in front! ⚽️Tidy finish from the Welshman... #EFL | #CarabaoCup | @LUFC pic.twitter.com/GzWg6zLGLm

Nottingham Forest 0 Leeds United 1 (James) We finally have a breakthrough. Kalimuendo gives the ball up cheaply in the middle of the park and Longstaff is there to pick up the pieces, darting infield before laying on a perfectly weighted for James to gallop on to, take a touch and sweep beyond Sels. The winger has been Leeds’ biggest threat and deserves that goal.

James finds space down the right - again - and his cross is closed down and deflected behind for a corner.

Longstaff’s floated delivery is tipped away by Sels, but it turns out that the ball went out before coming in so a Forest goal kick is awarded.

A lovely rendition of Mull of Kintyre precedes a short blast of the referee’s whistle and we’re back under way...

Schlager goes into the book instantly for grabbing a handful of Tanaka’s shirt as the Japan international attempted to escape his clutches.

This hasn’t been much of an improvement from Saturday.

Both teams are producing masterclasses in how to misplace passes. Oliver Glasner and Daniel Farke have spent much of the first half looking very frustrated.

James Trafford must be feeling very comfortable and confident of a second successive clean sheet after joining from Manchester City.

Let’s hope for an improvement in the second-half.

Should the scores remain level after 90 minutes, we will go straight to penalties. There’s still a half to play of course, but Forest’s League Cup shoot-out record should be a source of confidence having won seven from eight.

What a tackle from Joe Rodon! 💥#EFL | #CarabaoCup | @LUFC pic.twitter.com/p5GkzSFEoZ

James wins the ball on the halfway line and feeds Okafor down the left. He attempts a deft through-ball into a thicket of bodies but it comes to nothing.

Leeds circulate the ball, working the ball from side to side but there is nowhere near enough movement in front of the ball-player for any meaningful forward passes to be played.

And, quite aptly, the referee blows up at three seconds past 45 minutes. Certainly not a half for the books.

Another half-chance for Forest! Milenkovic lands on a second ball off a deep free-kick but he cannot keep his strike down. A classic centre-half’s effort if you will.

Ampadu comes over to the left to fire in a long throw-in. Sels comes steaming out of his goal and fumbles the ball but is awarded a free-kick after Muharemovic makes contact. Looked very minimal in all fairness.

Oof, a good chance for Aina! Williams’ cross from the left comes all the way through to his opposite wing-back, but Aina’s half-volley sails over. A cracking contact, though.

Elvedi and Muharemovic look to be astute buys from Leeds’ perspective. Both assured at the back and the latter especially is confident progressing the ball.

Just as I type that Forest threaten with a ball over the top, but Justin nips in to take the ball away from Wood.

Another decent opening for Leeds after a Forest turnover. Nmecha strides through the middle but Milenkovic is in position to ensure his run comes to nothing.

What a tackle! Kalimuendo bursts through the middle after Leeds cede possession in a dangerous position. The winger plays in Wood who looks to be through on goal but Rodon comes out of nowhere to telescope a limb and stop the forward in his tracks. Fantastic defensive work from the Welshman.

Nmecha attempts to break beyond the halfway line but is stymied by a swarm of Forest players. He demands a foul from the referee who is not interested in the least.

It’s then Okafor’s turn to put in a dangerous cross from the left, but Nmecha cannot get to it.

Tanaka becomes the first man to go into the book. The ball gets away from him and Jesus puts body between man and ball smartly to win the foul.

Tanaka is now dropping into the back line to allow Leeds’ defenders the licence to get wider and higher. Forest will need to be wary of their opponents’ numerical advantage down the flanks.

The game has reached something of a holding pattern as both sides resolve to slow things down, at least temporarily. Forest have settled into a slightly deeper block.

Sensing an opportunity, Ampadu spins in a glorious through-ball between centre-back and full-back for James to gallop on to. He hits the by-line and cuts back to Longstaff, but the midfielder can’t beat Sels. A good chance that probably should have been converted.

A good chance goes begging! 🫣Longstaff is free for Leeds but fires it straight at Sels...#EFL | #CarabaoCup pic.twitter.com/0UJdfSDQ6w

Tanaka then turns provider, winning possession in Forest’s half before playing in Longstaff, whose cross-cum-shot does not threaten Sels’ goal.

Both sides have physical, quick out-balls, which has made for a frenetic encounter thus far. James rasps in another fierce cross from the right after another sweeping Leeds move, but Nmecha cannot get there and Tanaka fires well over on the follow-up.

Aina’s throw-in, this time from the left, is flicked on to Jesus at the back post and while the forward is able to direct the ball goalwards there is Justin on the line to clear the ball to safety.

Chance! Dominguez slides in Aina down the right channel and the full-back’s mishit cross has Trafford scrambling. He palms the ball behind for a corner, which is headed away for a Forest throw-in on the far side.

Leeds are enjoying a spell of possession here, Tanaka and Longstaff peeling off into the wide areas to collect the ball and disrupt Forest’s mid-block out-of-possession structure. The hosts are more than happy for Leeds to circulate the ball in front of their first line of pressure as, for the second time tonight, Trafford boots it out into touch.

Dominguez stands up a smart cross to the far post where Aina is waiting to head back across goal. Trafford backpedals into Kalimuendo and the referee awards Leeds a free-kick.

Wonderful touch there early in the game from none other than Oliver Glasner.

Forest’s head coach perfectly trapped a high ball as it landed towards him in the technical area.

James shows off his speed for the first time tonight, accelerating down the right before fizzing a dangerous ball into the six-yard box but Forest clear their lines.

Sels goes long to Wood (feels like the right play given his attributes), James lands on the second ball but can only boot the ball into row Z to jeers from the home fans.

Aina launches a long throw-in from the right and it’s headed behind for a corner. Trafford punches the inswinging delivery away and Williams’ effort from the edge of the box sails well over.

Forest are in their red home shirts, kicking from left to right. Leeds are in their yellow away number. Same set-up as the weekend.

Players and mascots walk on to the City Ground turf. A place in the League Cup third round on the line.

Oliver Glasner breaks his silence on Nottingham Forest's record signing, Liam Delap 🚨He speaks to @gabrielclarke05 ahead of Forest's Carabao Cup tie against Leeds 🗣️ pic.twitter.com/8DlWMIzVS9

Reflecting on Saturday’s defeat by Leeds in his programme notes, Glasner wrote: “I saw plenty of encouraging signs from the team on Saturday and I felt we were a lot closer to scoring than we were conceding, especially in the second half. Unfortunately, the small margins were not on our side.

Previewing tonight’s League Cup match, Leeds head coach Daniel Farke said: “Our league win is good for our mood and confidence, but this is a ‘do or die’ cup game. Both teams will be motivated to progress, so I expect a tight game. It will be difficult to win on the road again against a tough opponent.”

When asked what winning a first trophy of his managerial career would mean to him, Farke added: “Well, we weren’t too far away last season. Overall, I would say my form in cup competitions hasn’t been too bad during my career. I’m a big believer in these competitions, I like the ‘do or die’ mentality. I would never say no to another good cup run.”

The hosts’ kits tonight will include Carabao Cup sleeve patches with the number four on them, in recognition of the club’s League Cup triumphs in 1978, 1979, 1989 and 1990.

This is Forest and Leeds Part 2, just four days after they clashed in the Premier League.

Daniel Farke ruined the Oliver Glasner welcoming party on Saturday with a 1-0 smash-and-grab victory at the death.

Both managers have gone relatively strong for this tie, with only a sprinkling of debuts.

Ousmane Diomande, the £34m signing from Sporting, makes his first appearance while there is a first start for Xaver Schlager.

Leeds have given a debut to Switzerland defender Nico Elvedi.

The big breaking news is that Forest are smashing their club record to sign Chelsea forward Liam Delap for £45m.

Delap will undergo a medical at Forest on Wednesday with the deal potentially rising to £50m after add-ons.

It eclipses the previous transfer record of £37.5m for winger Omari Hutchinson.

Oliver Glasner has prioritised the addition of a new centre-forward this summer and Delap ticks pretty much every box for him.

Farke makes six changes to the complement that started against Forest in the league on Saturday.

Our @Carabao_Cup XI this evening. 📋 pic.twitter.com/Wv918WJScj

Welcome to live coverage of the Carabao Cup second-round match between Nottingham Forest and Leeds United. This will be the sides’ second meeting at the City Ground in four days after Anton Stach’s late free-kick decided an attritional contest on the Premier League’s opening weekend. Forest’s new head coach Oliver Glasner is something of a cup specialist, though, with FA Cup, Europa League and Conference League titles to his name and he will relish the opportunity to right the wrongs of Saturday in front of the Forest faithful.

The Austrian is Forest’s fifth head coach in less than 12 months and he will look to arrest the churn by bringing to the City Ground the success he enjoyed with Crystal Palace. During pre-season, the Austrian moulded Forest into his preferred 3-4-3 shape, placing summer acquisition Ousmane Diomande alongside the existing central-defensive partnership of Murillo and Nikola Milenković. Here, Diomande gets his Forest debut and Glasner brings in talisman Chris Wood from the start.

Daniel Farke will have been delighted to see his Leeds side continue their excellent form in pre-season – which included victories over Liverpool, Red Bull Leipzig and Augsburg – into the season proper. Although Leeds arrive at the City Ground shorn of attacking options Wilfried Gnonto, Noah Okafor and Mateo Joseph through injury, Farke still shuffles the pack in the forward positions with this weekend’s visit of Brentford to Elland Road in mind.

#1497. Microbiome-wide PheWAS links gut microbial SNVs to health and exposures

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Alterations in the microbial composition of the human gut have been associated with a wide range of chronic diseases1,2. Yet species-level composition alone can obscure extensive within-species genetic diversity and functional variation. This has driven a shift towards strain-resolved, genetic-level analysis of the microbiome, leveraging microbial genetic variation to identify disease-relevant genes and pathways3,4,5,6. Here we conducted a phenome-wide association study (PheWAS) analysing 12.8 million gut microbial single-nucleotide variants (SNVs) with 244 host health phenotypes and environmental exposures in 10,781 individuals from 6 independent cohorts. We identify 940 independent associations across 69 host factors, including age, sex and cardiovascular and metabolic parameters. Structural analyses identified host-phenotype-associated SNVs in functionally important regions of proteins, findings that inform mechanistic hypotheses about how microbial genetic changes relate to environmental and host physiological factors. For example, we identified an age-associated SNV in Faecalibacterium prausnitzii that affects an amino acid within the protein pocket that binds glutathione. To support future efforts, all study summary statistics are provided in an online catalogue (https://fulab.web.rug.nl/SNV-MWAS/). Together, these results identify new biological connections between the human host and microbial genetic variants at base pair resolution and provide a resource for hypothesis generation that will aid future understanding of the strain-level functionality of the gut microbiota.

The gut microbiome exhibits large variations in its composition and genetic landscape. Within-species genetic variation underlies strain differences in fitness, metabolic capacities, pathogenicity and other biological properties. Thus, the field of microbiome research is moving towards strain-level or genetic-level dissection of the microbial contributions to human health (Supplementary Information). Structural variations in the gut microbiome have been linked to human body mass index (BMI), bile acid concentrations, the human plasma metabolome and host genetics, thereby identifying bacterial genes involved in glucose metabolism, bile acid biosynthesis and biotransformation, and N-acetylgalactosamine utilization3,4,5,6.

However, gut microbial genomes also contain abundant SNVs that can modulate microbial function and host interactions. For example, a SNV in the blc gene of Escherichia coli disrupts the intestinal barrier by decreasing the amount of lysophosphatidylethanolamine, a metabolite that aids remission of inflammatory bowel disease7. In the stomach, a SNV in Helicobacter pylori increases gastric cancer risk by enhancing the proteolytic activity of the serine protease HtrA (ref. 8). In Bacteroides coprocola, SNVs in glycosyl hydrolase genes have been associated with type 2 diabetes9. A SNV-based metagenome-wide association study (SNV-MWAS) in an Israeli population identified BMI-associated SNVs that were replicated in a geographically independent Dutch cohort10. Despite these examples, systematic explorations of the relationships between gut microbial SNVs and host phenotypes have not, to our knowledge, been carried out at phenome-wide scale. Such analyses require large-scale human cohort data with both metagenomic and deep phenotypic data, and they need to overcome a number of technical challenges. For example, microbial species exhibit complex population genetic structures, and these strong lineage effects may lead to false discoveries in association studies if population structure is not properly controlled.

In this study, we compiled shotgun metagenomic sequencing data of 11,831 faecal samples from 5 independent cohorts from the Netherlands and a cohort from Tanzania. Gut microbial genotypes were characterized using GT-Pro11, yielding 12.8 million SNVs in core genomic regions. We further developed a linear mixed-model (LMM)-based analysis workflow that controls for within-species population genetic structure to ensure that SNV–phenome associations detected are independent from the cumulative effect of strain lineage. We then conducted a PheWAS to identify associations between common metagenomic SNVs and 244 host phenotypic and exposure factors, using LMM in each cohort, followed by meta-analysis. In total, we detected 940 independent association signals supported by multiple cohorts that link 39,663 SNVs across 101 species to 69 host phenotypes or exposures, and the full set of results are available in an online catalogue. We also performed protein structural analyses to interpret the biological relevance of these associations.

We compiled faecal metagenomic sequencing data for 11,831 samples from 10,781 individuals from 6 cohorts (Fig. 1). Five cohorts are from the Netherlands—the Dutch Microbiome Project (DMP; n = 7,955)12, Lifelines-DEEP (LLD; n = 1,135, plus 340 followed up after an average of 4 years (designated LLD1 for baseline samples and LLD2 for follow-up samples))3,13, the 500-Functional Genomics Project (500FG; n = 529)14,15, the 1000 Inflammatory Bowel Disease Project (IBD; n = 544)16 and 300-Obesity (300OB; n = 298)15,17—and one is from Tanzania (300-Tanzania Functional Genomics Project (300TZFG), n = 320)18 (Fig. 1 and Supplementary Table 1). For LLD2 and 500FG, we have additional datasets from some of the same individuals (nLLD2 = 251, nFG500 = 459) with samples processed using both DNA extraction methods19 that allowed us to assess the effect of extraction protocol on SNV profiling and the robustness of microbial genotyping (Fig. 1, Supplementary Table 1 and Supplementary Note 1). The extensive phenotypic information for the corresponding samples was also curated and harmonized. We integrated 244 phenotypic and exposure factors (92 binary and 152 continuous or ordinal traits) available in the DMP or in at least 2 other cohorts for analysis (Fig. 2a and Supplementary Table 2). Among these, 131 phenotypes were available for at least 2 cohorts, whereas 113 were only available for the DMP. Across the whole dataset, the sample size per phenotype ranged from 593 to 11,706 (Supplementary Table 2).

In this study, we integrated whole-genome shotgun sequencing (WGS) data of 11,831 faecal samples from 10,781 individuals from 6 independent cohorts and harmonized 244 phenotype and exposure factors across these cohorts. Two of the six cohorts, Lifelines-DEEP (LLD) and 500-Functional Genomics (500FG), are represented by multiple datasets. n represents the number of faecal samples. LLD contains 1,135 samples collected at the study baseline time point (LLD1) and 340 samples collected for a subset of individuals at a follow-up time point after 4 years that were processed using two DNA isolation kits: 253 by QIAGEN QIAamp Fast DNA Stool Mini Kit (FSK; represented by circled F) (LLD2-FSK) and 338 using QIAGEN AllPrep DNA/RNA Mini Kit (APK; represented by circled A) (LLD2-APK). 500FG contains 529 samples that were also processed using the two DNA isolation kits: 517 processed using FSK (500FG-FSK) and 471 processed using APK (500FG-APK). To ensure sample independence in our downstream analysis, we used only LLD1 and 500FG-FSK in this analysis, and the additional datasets (LLD2-FSK, LLD2-APK and 500FG-APK) were used only to carry out technical assessments. We then conducted meta-genotyping for the WGS data from stool samples and generated the gut microbial genotype profile, keeping 12.8 million common biallelic microbial SNVs for the LMM-based SNV-MWAS. SNV-MWAS analyses were conducted separately for the six independent datasets from the six cohorts and then integrated through meta-analysis. Linkage disequilibrium-based grouping was conducted to extract independent signals, and an LMM-based permutation test was used to screen for robust association signals. To provide functional interpretation of SNV associations, we then carried out protein structural analysis. Created in BioRender; Fu, J. https://biorender.com/c1z5z7y (2026).

The numbers of species included were: DMP, n = 247; LLD1, n = 207; 500FG, n = 256; 300OB, n = 243; IBD, n = 154; and 300TZFG, n = 327. We genotyped 50,945,657 biallelic SNVs in the core genome of 881 species using GT-Pro11, which conducts reference-panel-based SNV detection using k-mer searching and exact matching. The number of SNVs detected in the DMP was higher than in other cohorts, probably owing to its larger sample size (Extended Data Fig. 1a,b). The total number of SNVs detected in at least 1 sample for each species ranged from 1 to 342,230 (mean = 58,131) (Extended Data Fig. 1c). The average density of SNVs in the core genomic region of gut bacteria was 32 SNVs per kilobase pair (Extended Data Fig. 1d), which is close to previous reports20. To keep only informative species for downstream analysis, we selected ‘common’ SNVs that were present in more than 10% of samples and had a minor allele frequency (MAF) of more than 5% in at least one cohort. Among the 50.95 million SNVs that were detected, 12,761,497 SNVs were common (Supplementary Table 3). As the distribution of common SNV counts per species was bimodal, with two peaks separated by approximately 1,000 SNVs (Extended Data Fig. 1e), we selected species with at least 1,000 common SNVs, resulting in 433 species with 12,706,564 common SNVs (Fig. 2b, Extended Data Fig. 1f,g and Supplementary Table 4). These 433 species collectively accounted for, on average, 84.3% (s.d. = 9.4%) of the total abundance of the gut microbial community. After filtering, 300TZFG had the highest number of species for analysis (327) and the most common SNVs (7,369,266) (Fig. 2b and Extended Data Fig. 1f–h). The average density of common SNV sites in the core genomic region of gut bacteria was 16 SNVs per kilobase pair (Extended Data Fig. 1i). The within-species population structure of the 433 species and the effect of technical factors are described extensively in Supplementary Notes 2 and 3 (Supplementary Figs. 1–4 and Supplementary Tables 5–8). We also pre-calculated the Bonferroni-controlled threshold for study-wide significance by dividing 0.05 by the total number of phenotype–SNV pairs tested (922,497,753), yielding a threshold of 5.42 × 10−11 (Methods).

To understand the functional consequences of SNVs, we annotated genes from reference genomes and predicted the potential functional effect of SNVs on bacterial gene products (synonymous, missense, start or stop codon, and non-protein-coding)21 (Fig. 2c, Extended Data Fig. 2 and Supplementary Table 9). Most SNVs (11,819,660, 93.02%) were located in protein-coding regions, including 9,579,907 (75.39%) synonymous, 2,216,969 (17.45%) missense and 22,784 (0.18%) start or stop codon variants (Fig. 2c). The distribution of the proportion of codon-altering SNVs (missense or start or stop codon SNVs) varied across different bacterial species (Extended Data Fig. 2), reflecting the genetic diversity and evolutionary pressures experienced by these species.

We next performed an SNV-MWAS of 244 factors by linking them to 12 million common SNVs using LMMs fitted separately for each species, phenotype and cohort. These LMMs controlled for population structure by including the species-level between-sample genetic linkage matrix as a random effect. Age, sex, species abundance and clean read count were included as fixed-effect covariates, except in the analyses for age and sex themselves. Given that reference and alternative alleles may coexist within a sample with differing abundances, we encoded gut microbial genotypes as a dosage value ranging from 0 to 1 to represent the frequency of the alternative allele.

Following the per-cohort SNV-MWAS, we conducted a meta-analysis weighted by sample size for the SNV–phenotype pairs available in at least two cohorts to integrate the SNV-MWAS results derived from different cohorts (Fig. 1). This included only the independent datasets—that is, excluding LLD2 and 500FG-APK. This analysis identified 49,346 significant and robust associations that passed the study-wide significance cut-off (meta-analysis P < 5.42 × 10−11; Extended Data Fig. 3 and Methods) and were supported by at least 2 cohorts based on a permutation-based robustness test (cohort permutation P < 0.05 with 999 permutations), with the same association direction. These associations involved 39,663 SNVs of 101 species and 69 phenotypes.

As a resource for further validation and hypothesis generation, we have constructed a catalogue (https://fulab.web.rug.nl/SNV-MWAS/) that includes all 49,346 robust associations as well as the suggestive signals that passed the species-wide significance level (species-specific, defined by Bonferroni correction based on the number of tested SNVs within each species; Methods) in the meta-analysis and the largest cohort DMP (see examples in Supplementary Note 4 and Supplementary Fig. 5).

Most SNV associations (85.76%) were supported by two cohorts, and 14.24% were supported by three or more cohorts (Fig. 3a). Although all associated SNVs showed a similar ratio of start or stop codon or missense SNVs (17.49%) compared with the background (all common SNVs), six phenotypes were significantly enriched for start or stop codon or missense SNVs (χ2 test P < 0.05): Lifelines protein diet score, on-a-diet behaviour during the past month, thrombocyte count, waist circumference, β-blocker intake and sex (Extended Data Fig. 4). SNVs in the non-coding region may affect gene expression through upstream regulators. For example, variants located approximately 10 bp upstream of the start codon may affect the ribosome-binding site or other elements involved in translation initiation, thereby altering bacterial protein expression22. We further examined the distribution patterns of common and phenotype-associated SNVs in gene upstream regions. The common SNV count showed a drop in −10 bp regions (Fig. 3b), and the ratio of SNVs with at least one association showed an uneven distribution, with a drop at −11 bp and two peaks at −55 bp and −83 bp (Fig. 3c).

As SNVs can be correlated due to linkage disequilibrium in the genomes, we conducted a grouping analysis to select the most significant SNVs within each linkage disequilibrium block as representative tags of the independent signals (between-SNV r2 < 0.01; Methods). We then identified 940 independent SNV-MWAS signals (Fig. 3d,e and Supplementary Table 10) and 13,198 SNVs with a high probability of contribution to phenotypic variation (posterior inclusion probability > 0.8) (Supplementary Note 5 and Supplementary Fig. 6). Power assessment found that 70.5% of signals have more than 0.80 power to be detected given the observed effect size, sample size, and MAF (Supplementary Note 6 and Supplementary Fig. 7) and showed a negative correlation between MAF and effect size (Fig. 3f, R = −0.29, P = 6.06 × 10−20). We also assessed replication across cohorts of different ancestries. Among the 940 signals, 215 had both SNVs and phenotypes available in the Dutch and Tanzanian cohorts, with 161 (74.9%) signals involving 8 different phenotypes supported by both cohorts. For example, 48 association signals of 23 species with age are supported by Dutch and Tanzanian cohorts (Extended Data Fig. 5).

Notably, among the 940 SNV–phenotype association signals, 65.74% showed no significant associations at the abundance level (linear regression, Bonferroni-corrected meta-analysis P > 0.05; Fig. 3d,e). To illustrate the added value of SNV associations, we systematically assessed the phenotypic associations with the gut microbiome at the species abundance, SNV and structural variant levels. Among the 62,464 species–phenotype pairs (Methods), 533 showed associations at SNV level, 460 (86.30%) showed associations only at SNV level, and just 5 (0.9%) showed associations at all 3 levels (Extended Data Fig. 6 and Supplementary Tables 11–13). These results suggest that SNV-based analyses provide complementary information to structural variant- and abundance-based analyses when investigating host–microbiome associations4,5,23.

Among 940 signals, 810 were linked with intrinsic factors and 130 with exposure factors (Supplementary Note 7). We found 152 pairwise signal combinations involving 26 intrinsic phenotypes (excluding age, sex and height), in which the same tag SNVs were associated with 1 or more exposure factors (Fig. 3g and Supplementary Table 14). To assess whether exposure factors confounded the association signals of the intrinsic factors, we included the exposure factors as covariates in a robust association test using LMM-based permutation tests (999 permutations) for the association signals shared between intrinsic phenotypes and exposure factors. Owing to data completeness requirements (phenotype, exposure and SNV all had to be observed in at least 100 samples), we could evaluate 66 signals. Of these, 54 (81.8%) remained significant in at least 2 cohorts after controlling for the exposure factors (permutation P < 0.05), suggesting that the exposure factors did not confound the majority of the SNV associations with intrinsic phenotypes.

Age showed the highest number of association signals (99 signals) involving 8,117 SNVs across 42 species (meta-analysis P < 5.42 × 10−11) (Fig. 3d and Supplementary Table 10). We next assessed how well microbial SNVs could predict host age (Methods). To this end, we trained a machine learning model in the DMP cohort and evaluated its predictive performance in the other cohorts. The model explained 12.8–42.0% of the variation in age (R2) in the test datasets (Supplementary Notes 8 and 9, Supplementary Figs. 8–10 and Supplementary Tables 15 and 16), suggesting the predictive potential of gut microbial genetics for host age.

The most robust signal was supported by four independent cohorts (meta P < 5.42 × 10−11; Fig. 4a, Extended Data Fig. 7 and Supplementary Table 10). This signal contains five SNVs in the genome of F. prausnitzii_I (species ID: 102274), and their associations were not confounded by other microbial features, including bacterial lineage, species abundance and structural variants (Extended Data Fig. 8 and Supplementary Note 10). Notably, all five age-associated SNVs are missense variants located in the sarA_2 gene (gene ID: 102274_01471). The most significant SNV was 102274_1617247 (effect allele: T, effect allele frequency = 17.38%, β = 4.93, meta-analysis P = 1.00 × 10−17), showing that individuals carrying the T allele were 4.9 ± 0.6 years older (mean ± s.d.) than those without the T allele (Supplementary Table 10). The linkage disequilibrium analysis showed that the lead SNV 102274_1617247 is linked with the other four missense SNVs (R2 > 0.2; Fig. 4a,b) in sarA_2, and significant signals were detected in all cohorts except 300OB (Fig. 4c,d). Notably, all 300OB participants are older than 50 years and show a higher frequency of age-associated alleles compared with the other four Dutch cohorts, which have younger average ages (Extended Data Fig. 9). In other words, the age-associated allele in the sarA_2 gene of F. prausnitzii_I was enriched in an older population. Moreover, replication of the association across the Dutch and Tanzanian cohorts (Fig. 4d) suggests convergent genetic changes during host ageing in different ethnic groups.

The sarA_2 gene is a homologue of the oppA gene, which encodes an oligopeptide-binding lipoprotein with a Tat pathway signal sequence in its N terminus. The protein product of sarA_2 also forms an outer-membrane unit of an ATP-binding cassette (ABC)-type transporter system responsible for the uptake of oligopeptides—the oligopeptide permease (OPP) complex (Fig. 4b). We thus hypothesized that the age-associated missense SNVs may influence the function of the SarA_2 protein (also known as OppA). To test this, we assembled the OPP complex based on the AlphaFold3 prediction, including the five subunits encoded by sarA, oppB_4, oppC_4, oppD_4 and oppF_4 (Fig. 4e). This structural comparative analysis revealed that the predicted OPP structure is similar to the substrate-binding protein-dependent ABC transporter systems of Mycobacterium tuberculosis H37Rv (Protein Data Bank (PDB): 8JA7)24 and E. coli (PDB: 6CVL)25, supporting the plausibility of the predicted ABC transporter architecture. The sectional view of the predicted OPP complex structure revealed a tunnel-like cavity, with the OppA subunit acting as a gate for the transportation tunnel (Fig. 4e). Notably, the age-associated SNVs we identify are located in the cavity of OppA that relates to the tunnel (Fig. 4f), which suggests that these SNVs may affect the transportation function of the protein complex.

To infer the potential ligand of the OPP complex and better understand the underlying age-related changes in transport function, we examined the functional annotations of each subunit of the complex in detail. The OppF_4 subunit, encoded by the gene 102274_01467, was annotated as a GsiA subunit of the transporter for glutathione, an antioxidant that can prevent the damage caused by oxidative stress for both eukaryotes and prokaryotes. We then compared the protein sequences of OppA, OppB_4, OppC_4, OppD_4 and OppF_4 with 3,239 existing protein sequences of the ABC-type glutathione transport system and found that all 5 subunits match existing protein sequences (E-value < 1 × 10−10; Methods), indicating that the OPP complex may function as a glutathione transport system. In silico molecular docking analysis further revealed that glutathione can bind to the pocket region of the OppA protein (Fig. 4g and Extended Data Fig. 10). This suggests that age-associated mutations may affect glutathione uptake efficiency and help F. prausnitzii_I better resist ageing-related oxidative stress in the intestinal environment.

Motivated by the structural characterization of age-associated SNVs in sarA_2, we further systematically depicted the effect of associated SNVs in relation to protein structures. To this end, we focused on 6,799 associated missense SNVs, which are related to 3,724 proteins. We retrieved high-confidence three-dimensional structures of 2,141 (57.49%) proteins with 3,705 associated missense SNVs from the ESM Metagenomic Atlas26 and AlphaFoldDB27. We then systematically characterized these SNVs in relation to structural properties, including relative solvent accessibility (RSA, how exposed a residue is to a solvent), distance to ligand (DTL, distance from the residue to the nearest predicted pocket centre) and distance to protein–protein interaction interface (DTPPI, distance to the closest residue within a predicted protein–protein interface region) (Methods). We designated SNVs in low-DTPPI regions (DTPPI < 10 Å) or low-DTL regions (DTL < 15 Å) as structurally important28,29,30,31,32. Out of 3,705 SNVs, 752 (20.3%) were structurally important by these criteria, including 246 and 528 SNVs affecting amino acid residues in low-DTL and low-DTPPI regions, respectively (Fig. 5a and Supplementary Table 17). These SNVs were associated with 40 different phenotypes (Fig. 5b,c).
